'''Buro Happold Limited''' (previously ''BuroHappold Engineering'') is a British professional services firm that provides [[engineering]] consultancy, [[design]], planning, project management, and consulting services for buildings, infrastructure, and the environment. It was founded in [[Bath, Somerset]], in 1976 by Sir [[Edmund Happold]] when he took up a post at the [[University of Bath]] as Professor of [[Architecture]] and Engineering Design.

Originally working mainly on projects in the [[Middle East]], the firm now operates worldwide and in almost all areas of engineering for the [[built environment]], working in 24 locations around the world.

==Sir Edmund Happold==
{{Main|Edmund Happold}}

Edmund (or Ted) Happold worked at [[Arup Group Limited|Arup]] before founding Buro Happold, where he worked on projects such as the [[Sydney Opera House]] and the [[Pompidou Centre]]. Ted Happold was renowned{{By whom|date=May 2026}} within the field of lightweight and [[tensile structure]]s. As a result, Buro Happold has undertaken a large number of [[tensile structure|tensile]] and other lightweight structures since its founding (including the [[Millennium Dome]]). Ted Happold died in 1996, but the firm claims to maintain his views on engineering and life.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Sharpe|first1=Dennis|title=OBITUARY: Professor Sir Edmund Happold|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituary-professor-sir-edmund-happold-1324558.html|access-date=20 September 2017|work=Independent|date=18 January 1996|archive-date=21 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170921051652/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituary-professor-sir-edmund-happold-1324558.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

The King's Office, Council of Ministers and Majlis Al Shura ([[Qasr Al Hukm District|KOCOMMAS]]), Central Government Complex in [[Riyadh]], Saudi Arabia was the firm's first major design project in 1976.<ref name=timeline/> Initially, Buro Happold offered only [[structural engineering]] [[consultancy]], with a particular strength in [[tensile structure|lightweight structures]], but in 1977 it added [[civil engineering]] and [[geotechnical engineering]] and in 1978 building services engineering.<ref name=timeline/>   In 1982, Buro Happold started to work with Future Tents Ltd (FTL) on a variety of temporary and recreational structures. The firms combined their operations in 1992, but split again in 1997.

By 1993, Buro Happold had 130 employees and eight partners. In 1998, this had grown to 300 employees and 12 partners, while in 2000 with over 500 employees the partnership was increased to 23.<ref name=timeline/> In 2006, the partnership stood at 25 with over 1,400 employees and 14 offices. Due to this growth and the addition of so many different services, the company was restructured in 2003 to consist of multi-disciplinary teams of engineers, each with structural, mechanical and electrical engineers supported by specialist consulting groups.<ref name=timeline/>

In 2005, Buro Happold launched Happold Consulting, a management and overseas development consultancy with expertise in the construction sector, and Happold Media, a subsidiary offering graphic design and media development services.

==Projects==

===Lightweight structures===
[[File:Masjed Nabawi Sahn.jpg|thumb|left|Umbrella-like shading canopies inside the [[Al-Masjid al-Nabawi|Masjid an-Nabawi (Mosque of the Prophet)]]]]

In 1973, before the founding of Buro Happold, [[Edmund Happold]], [[Ian Liddell]], Vera Straka, [[Peter Rice (structural engineer)|Peter Rice]] and [[Michael Dickson (engineer)|Michael Dickson]] established a lightweight structures research laboratory corresponding to Frei Otto's similar research institute at the university of [[Stuttgart]]. Ted Happold was the first to introduce ethylenetetrafluoroethylene ([[ETFE]]) as a cladding material, and the outcomes of the research carried out by the laboratory led to the development of the designs for the Mannheim Multihall gridshell and a number of landmark fabric structures in the Middle East and the UK, allowing the new building forms to become generally accepted by architects and clients.<ref name="Nina Rappaport"/>

Buro Happold's early projects included designing giant fabric umbrellas for [[Pink Floyd]] concerts,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.stufish.com/Pages/Dinosaur/Pink%20Floyd/Animals%20Tour/Pink%20Floyd%20Animals%20Concert%20Tour%201977%2001.html |title=Pink Floyd Animals Concert Tour 1977 |publisher=Stufish |access-date=22 March 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070224074411/http://www.stufish.com/Pages/Dinosaur/Pink%20Floyd/Animals%20Tour/Pink%20Floyd%20Animals%20Concert%20Tour%201977%2001.html |archive-date=24 February 2007 }}</ref> the Munich Aviary and the [[Mannheim Multihalle]], both with [[Frei Otto]], an architect who repeatedly worked with Buro Happold on projects which pioneered lightweight structures. The Mannheim Multihalle was a timber [[gridshell]] of {{convert|50|x|50|mm|abbr=in}} lathes of hemlock of irregular form, depending on the elasticity of spring washers at the joints for its flexible form. It was one of the first major uses of structural gridshells.<ref name="Nina Rappaport"/>

[[File:Expo2000 venezuela1.jpg|thumb|The [[Venezuela]] Pavilion at [[Expo 2000]] in [[Hanover]], consisting of fabric 'petals' which could open and close according to weather conditions]]

Following the development of fabric structures expertise on the projects with Frei Otto, Buro Happold was instrumental in further developing the knowledge and technology of fabric structures. With [[Bodo Rasch]], a protégé of [[Frei Otto]], and drawing on experience from the Pink Floyd canopies, they designed folding, umbrella-like canopies to shade the courtyard of [[Al-Masjid al-Nabawi|Al-Masjid al-Nabawi (The Mosque of the Prophet)]] in [[Medina]], Saudi Arabia.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eC074cyRyI|title=Youtube Video of canopies closing|website=[[YouTube]]|access-date=25 November 2016|archive-date=21 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161121105921/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eC074cyRyI|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://archnet.org/library/images/thumbnails.jsp?location_id=2951 |title=Archnet Gallery of Prophet's Mosque |publisher=Archnet |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081205101057/http://archnet.org/library/images/thumbnails.jsp?location_id=2951 |archive-date= 5 December 2008 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.anwary-islam.com/medina-pic/nabwi-umb_b4.htm |title=Medina's Gallery |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071026224357/http://www.anwary-islam.com/medina-pic/nabwi-umb_b4.htm |archive-date=26 October 2007 }}</ref> They also designed the, at the time, largest fabric canopy in Europe at the [[Ashford Designer Outlet]] in the UK.<ref>Walker. 1998. p.69</ref>

This development of fabric structures expertise culminated in Buro Happold, with a team led by [[Ian Liddell]], and with Paul Westbury,<ref name=westbury>{{cite journal|title=Ingenia Magazine: An Intuitive Engineer|url=http://www.ingenia.org.uk/ingenia/issues/issue31/Issue31_Profile.pdf|author=Michael Kenward OBE|issue=31|date=June 2007|access-date=30 November 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080410220727/http://www.ingenia.org.uk/ingenia/issues/issue31/Issue31_Profile.pdf|archive-date=10 April 2008|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref> designing the [[Millennium Dome]], the world's largest fabric roof and the first building of its type.<ref name=dome>{{cite web|url=http://www.raeng.org.uk/prizes/macrobert/winners/win1999.htm|title=MacRobert Award 1999 Winner|publisher=Royal Academy of Engineers|access-date=29 November 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081205034551/http://www.raeng.org.uk/prizes/macrobert/winners/win1999.htm|archive-date=5 December 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref> The expertise in wooden gridshell structures has resulted in the design of structures such as the [[Weald and Downland Gridshell|Weald and Downland Museum]] and the [[Savill Building]] in [[Windsor Great Park]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.burohappold.com/projects/savill-building/ |title=Savill Building |publisher=Buro Happold |access-date=16 January 2008 |archive-date=16 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161116101817/http://www.burohappold.com/projects/savill-building/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The Savill Gardens Gridshell, Glen Howells Architects|url=http://www.fourthdoor.org/annular/?page_id=453|publisher=Fourth Door|access-date=20 September 2017|archive-date=21 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170921050228/http://www.fourthdoor.org/annular/?page_id=453|url-status=live}}</ref>

Buro Happold has also completed the designs of a number of cardboard structures, notably the Japan Pavilion for [[Expo 2000]] in [[Hanover]] with [[Shigeru Ban]] and Frei Otto, consisting of a gridshell of paper tubes (the structure was reinforced with steel in order to comply with fire regulations, though the tubular structure was itself structurally sufficient).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.building.co.uk/story.asp?storyCode=3047276|title=The man with the golden pen. issue 08|publisher=Building Magazine|date=2005 }}</ref> The firm has worked with Shigeru Ban on a number of other projects. Another design in cardboard was the Westborough School cardboard classroom in Westcliff.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cardboardschool.co.uk/|title=Cardboard classroom|publisher=Westborough School|access-date=22 December 2006|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070103145819/http://www.cardboardschool.co.uk/|archive-date=3 January 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Awards==

===Notable awards===

[[File:Savill Building front.jpg|The [[Savill Building]], a visitor centre at Windsor Great Park|thumb|center|upright=3.6]]

Buro Happold's most recent awards include: ‘Building performance consultancy (over 1000 employees)’ and the 'Energy Efficient Product or Innovation' Award for NewMass,<ref>{{Cite web |title=NewMass System |url=https://www.burohappold.com/projects/newmass-system/ |website=Buro Happold}}</ref> a phase change chilled beam at the 2018 CIBSE Building Performance Awards.{{citation needed|date=September 2020}}

Buro Happold won the [[Aga Khan Award for Architecture]] for [[Tuwaiq Palace]] in [[Riyadh]] in 1998 and again in 2010 for the design of the [[Wadi Hanifah]] wetlands.<ref>[http://archrecord.construction.com/news/daily/archives/2010/11/101124aga_khan.asp Jenna M. McKnight: ''Revealed: Winners of 2010 Aga Khan Award for Architecture'', in the Architectural Record, 24 November 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150907002539/http://archrecord.construction.com/news/daily/archives/2010/11/101124aga_khan.asp |date=7 September 2015 }}, retrieved 1 December 2010</ref> Buro Happold also won the [[Queen's Award for Enterprise]] twice, for export achievement and again for [[sustainable development]].  In 1999 Buro Happold engineers [[Ian Liddell]], Paul Westbury, Dawood Pandor and technician Gary Dagger won the [[Royal Academy of Engineering]]'s [[MacRobert Award]] for their design of the [[Millennium Dome]] – only the second time in the award's history that it has gone to a construction project.<ref>{{cite press release|url=http://www.raeng.org.uk/news/releases/shownews.htm?NewsID=75|title=Millennium Dome shows it's not just a pretty space|publisher=Royal Academy of Engineering|date=1999-10-25|access-date=2007-12-10|archive-date=12 June 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110612045555/http://www.raeng.org.uk/news/releases/shownews.htm?NewsID=75|url-status=live}}</ref> Buro Happold received the accompanying gold medal.<ref name="dome" />

In 2007, Buro Happold won the [[Structural Awards|IStructE Supreme Award]] for the [[Savill Building]] in [[Windsor Great Park]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.istructe.org/StructuralAwards/2007/category00/projects.asp |title=Structural Awards website |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716071301/http://www.istructe.org/StructuralAwards/2007/category00/projects.asp |archive-date=16 July 2011 }}</ref>

The [[Aviva Stadium]] won the 2011 International Project Award at the [[British Construction Industry Awards]]. The [[Royal Shakespeare Theatre]] won the Project of the Year Award at the 2011 Building Awards. At the 2010 [[Structural Awards]] the John Hope Gateway building won the award for Arts or Entertainment Structures.
The Institution of Structural Engineers announced there were to be two winners of its coveted Gold Medal in 2012: Buro Happold's then-CEO Paul Westbury was one of them. Paul was selected for the award due to his innovation in the structural form, and design of sports and entertainment buildings; in particular for his leading contribution to the design and construction of Arsenal's Emirates Stadium in London, the 2006 Olympic Speed Skating Oval in Turin, Dublin's Aviva Stadium and the London 2012 Olympic Stadium.

===Stirling Prize winning projects===

[[File:Magna Science Adventure Centre.jpg|right|The [[Magna Science Adventure Centre]], [[Rotherham]]|thumb|upright]]

extract:
Buro Happold Limited (previously BuroHappold Engineering) is a British professional services firm that provides engineering consultancy, design, planning, project management, and consulting services for buildings, infrastructure, and the environment. It was founded in Bath, Somerset, in 1976 by Sir Edmund Happold when he took up a post at the University of Bath as Professor of Architecture and Engineering Design.
Originally working mainly on projects in the Middle East, the firm now operates worldwide and in almost all areas of engineering for the built environment, working in 24 locations around the world.
